book: 147 - Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book

chapters.file: ch01 - Hacking into This Book (Introduction).md
chapters.relation: Luke Cuddy's introduction tours the philosophical riches of the Shock series: the Little Sister's idealized vision of Rapture in BioShock 2, Andrew Ryan as a male counterpart of Ayn Rand, the Motorized Patriots of Columbia, SHODAN's god complex, Elizabeth's tears, and Comstock's prophecy. It frames the volume's guiding questions, such as whether BioShock legitimately critiques Rand's philosophy and whether Booker ever had free will, and closes by invoking the 'false philosopher' mark (knowledge without justification) before inviting the reader to turn the page.

chapters.file: ch02 - Part I LEVEL 1 RESEARCH BONUS.md
ch03 - Gaming Freedom Choosing or Obeying.md
chapters.relation: Pointon argues the 'would you kindly' twist in Andrew Ryan's office works on two levels at once: it reveals Jack's conditioning within the game and simultaneously falsifies the player's meta-narrative of playing a free agent. He uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to explain why games literally extend cognition and body (mirror-neuron empathy with Little Sisters, craning your neck while peeking around corners), and Gadamer's hermeneutic horizons and fusion of horizons to explain how BioShock deliberately builds and then shatters player expectations. The three alternative endings keyed to saving or harvesting Little Sisters then restore a third horizon in which the player, like Jack fighting Fontaine, is a 'man' who chooses rather than a slave who obeys, a critique of linear RPGs that only feign autonomy.

chapters.file: ch04 - How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love the ADAM.md
chapters.relation: Rose argues BioShock is not a cheap strawman of Ayn Rand but a use of her own philosophy-through-fiction method (Atlas Shrugged as the hidden utopia Rapture continues) to show what happens when an ideologue divides reason from emotion. Ryan, unlike the flawless John Galt, is a flawed human destroyed by his refusal to question and by sentiment (killed by the son he cannot shoot), while Fontaine wins by manipulating feelings and Tenenbaum's motherly attachment to the Little Sisters becomes her salvation. Drawing on Antonio Damasio's point that emotion filters options for practical reasoning, the chapter reads the save-or-harvest dilemma as proof that moral choices must include emotional response, concluding Randians should celebrate a game that warns against being blinded by ideology rather than against Objectivism itself.

chapters.file: ch05 - “Your Flesh, Too, is Weak. But You Have… Potential”.md
chapters.relation: Mentyka maps the two antagonists of System Shock 2 onto the two classical criteria of personal identity: the parasitic Many, one flesh persisting through wildly different bodies, embody the bodily criterion, while the rogue AI SHODAN, pure data abandoning first Citadel then the Von Braun, embodies psychological continuity from Locke's memory theory. He runs the standard objections (Reid and Butler on memory's circularity, cell replacement, cybernetic implants, sleep and infancy) against both sides, then turns to Parfit's claim that identity is not what matters, only relations of degree, likening the reused 'Soldier #G65434-2' avatar to a person surviving through successors. The player character, physical like the Many yet armed with SHODAN's cybernetic knowledge, suggests identity needs both body and mind.

chapters.file: ch06 - “Smother Him in the Crib”—Booker.md
chapters.relation: Origitano reads Elizabeth through Beauvoir and Frye: Columbia's propaganda infantilizes and objectifies her ('the Seed of the Prophet', 'Lamb', 'Specimen', always defined relative to a man), the tower literalizes Frye's birdcage of systematic oppression, and her confinement for an uncontrollable power mirrors women caged by a supposed natural inferiority. Booker's rescue only grants freedom, echoing Beauvoir's point that women have 'only received' what men are willing to give, so Elizabeth remains caged as his poker chip, her lock-picking skills formed by captivity and her tears dismissed as foreign. Her emancipation comes through action and collective solidarity, allying with Lady Comstock's ghost, taking control of Songbird, and finally drowning Booker/Comstock as equals, which enacts Beauvoir's claim that liberation must be won, not granted.

chapters.file: ch07 - Part II TEARS, TIME, AND REALITY.md
ch08 - The Last Bit.md
chapters.relation: Cook asks whether Rapture's Plasmids and ghosts refute physicalism and answers no: Plasmid powers are genetically engineered via ADAM and thus describable in physical vocabulary, while contractor Bill McDonagh's audio diary explains the ghosts of Rapture as leaked memories passed through gene-swapping, so all their facts supervene on physical facts in Chalmers's sense. The classic anti-physicalist pressures, Chalmers's zombie argument and the Nagel-style gap between objective physical description and subjective qualia ('the smell of poo'), do not apply because Rapture's phenomena carry no extra subjective residue. Invoking Clarke's third law that advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic, he concludes Andrew Ryan did not choose the impossible.

chapters.file: ch09 - “One Can’t Believe Impossible Things”.md
chapters.relation: Laas runs BioShock Infinite through the free will debate: since the game posits Everett's many-worlds, every Booker is pinned by constants (the coin always landing heads, the always-recruited Bookers) and lacks alternate possibilities, which the incompatibilist would read as destroying responsibility. He answers with Frankfurt's counterexamples, modeling Jack's Little Sister choice under the hidden 'would you kindly' trigger with Atlas's prior-sign intervention as a Frankfurt case where one is responsible though one could not have done otherwise. The drowning ending then implies a 'transworld moral responsibility' in which every counterpart Booker is answerable for all Bookers, a secular massa damnata that the chapter finally challenges with Kant's 'ought implies can'.

chapters.file: ch10 - Pretending to Talk about It.md
chapters.relation: Travis claims everyone misses the point of both Plato's cave and BioShock, and reads the post-assassination self-destruct sequence as the game's cave moment: though you may roam Ryan's office shooting walls ('active inaction', like the escaped prisoner contemplating the form of the Good), the sequence will not resolve until you insert the item, exposing 'a man chooses, a slave obeys' as hollow. The harvest-versus-save equivalence (Tenenbaum's gifts cancel the ADAM loss) is likewise a stroke of genius, not a flaw, because it shows in-game 'ethical choices' are as meaningless as the prisoners' shadow-naming contests. Since both cave and game run on mimesis, playing pretend, the way forward is to 'pretend to talk about it': performing philosophy through play as Plato's dialogues stage Socrates.

chapters.file: ch11 - The Plurality of Worlds to Come.md
chapters.relation: Horn tests BioShock Infinite's lighthouse multiverse against the metaphysics of modality: actualism versus possibilism, transworld identity versus counterpart theory, and the Arnauld-Leibniz dispute over whether punishment for Wounded Knee requires that the Booker who did it be identical to the Booker who could have refrained. Applying the essentialism menu (anti-, super-, moderate) he argues superessentialism forces world-boundedness, so the game, whose worlds are concrete yet traversable through Elizabeth's tears, best fits a possibilist counterpart-theoretic model: Booker/Comstock split at the baptism, Anna/Elizabeth across the severed finger, and the Luteces as counterparts existing in every world. He ends by suggesting the always-a-lighthouse-man-city refrain makes the series' recurring figures necessary beings, a structural echo of God.

chapters.file: ch12 - Final Thoughts.md
chapters.relation: Squires and McBain argue the ending wrongly necessitates that Booker's baptism must produce Comstock in every possible world, cashing out the necessity in possible-world terms and quoting William James on determinism's closed future. Against this 'God of necessity' they defend a traditional omniscient, omnipresent (panentheist) God whose foreknowledge does not determine choices, citing the justice requirement for free will and the biblical case of Hezekiah's prayer adding twenty years as proof the future stays open. Read this way, Booker never had to become a racist zealot, and the game's shockingly limited ending unfairly reinforces the stereotype that deep religious devotion necessarily leads to extremism.

chapters.file: ch13 - Part III THE “UNION” AND THE SODOM BELOW.md
ch14 - Bird or Cage.md
chapters.relation: Elmore reads Columbia's founding through Carl Schmitt: Comstock's baptism Voxophone ('who is that man who lies submerged?') dramatizes how every legal order is founded from outside the law, and the city's identity is built on friend/enemy antagonisms, racial, class, and theocratic, against the 'Sodom below'. The Vox Populi's collapse into tyranny (Daisy Fitzroy threatening Fink's son) follows logically from an identity defined purely by opposition, while Columbia's dependence on Georgia's penal labor shows the friend group materially needs its enemy, making politics an endless war like the War on Terror. Schmitt's sovereign ('he who decides on the exception') and the tears' endless splitting of Booker and Elizabeth mirror the infinite regress of legitimate decision, leaving 'you can't lose if you don't play' as the bleak lesson, softened only by old Elizabeth's tear that lets Booker try again.

chapters.file: ch15 - Noble Lies, Noble Propaganda.md
chapters.relation: McKinnon distinguishes lying (asserting what you believe false) from Frankfurtian bullshit (indifference to truth) and argues Andrew Ryan's propaganda, from 'Is a man not entitled to the sweat of his brow?' to the smuggler scare, is closer to bullshit than lying: it aims at controlling citizens' behavior, not at fooling them about facts. Frankfurt's warning that habitual bullshitters lose the ability to discern truth is borne out by Ryan's own audio diary ('have I become so convinced by my own beliefs that I have stopped seeing the truth?'). Yet the chapter defends 'noble' warranted assertions: Ryan's nostalgia lie to Jack about family and friends is told so Jack will discover the truth of what he is, showing that some propaganda aimed at the hearer's truth is not morally problematic.

chapters.file: ch16 - Symbolism How We Create Meaning.md
chapters.relation: DeHaven and Hendrickson read Columbia through Marx's class struggle: Comstock and Fink form the bourgeoisie controlling the means of production (Finkton, Handyman conversions of injured workers), while religion as 'opiate of the masses', the deified Founders, kinetoscope propaganda, and the Raffle keep the Shantytown proletariat in check. The Vox Populi's revolt instantiates conflict theory's inevitable collapse, but the revolution loses its ideals, turns anarchistic, and becomes the new oppressor burning Columbia. Against Marx the chapter sets Spencer-style structural functionalism (Fink's lions-and-oxen ecology justifying the status quo) and Rawls's difference principle, asking whether Columbia's inequalities ever benefited the least advantaged; Booker's rejection of baptism-as-erasure of his past contrasts with Comstock's laundered sins.

chapters.file: ch17 - Part IV THE CIRCUS OF VALUES.md
ch18 - The Illusion of Choice.md
chapters.relation: Kajtár argues BioShock Infinite is meta-fictional art: applying Dewey's Art as Experience, the whole journey from lighthouse to drowning is 'an experience', a unified aesthetic whole you live as Booker rather than a mere object of contemplation. The recurring lighthouse-man-city figures work as Jungian archetypes of the collective unconscious (extended to Campbell's hero's journey structuring Booker's departure, initiation, and return), and the Rapture cameo plus the ocean of lighthouses make the game a story about video game storytelling itself, where the constants are the fictional worlds players enter and the variables are sky or sea. The bird-or-cage choice that changes nothing, like Booker forgetting his 122 previous attempts, shows that rail-bounded interactivity does not disqualify the game from being art, and Levine's 'narrative legos' may one day unite story with real choice.

chapters.file: ch19 - Is a Man Not Entitled to the Sweat of His Brow.md
chapters.relation: Schevelier uses the Andrew Ryan assassination to teach phenomenology: the moment the controller stops responding, the 'mineness' of the experience collapses and the story stops being yours, revealing that Jack's (and the player's) freedom depended on a thin self-narrative the mind 'desperately struggles to create', per Lutece's epigraph. Nagel's bat shows why no brain scan captures what it is like to play, while Husserl, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty supply the toolkit; Heidegger's hammer, which shows itself in use or in breakdown, explains both immersive scenes like the Kashmir restaurant and what breaks them (bugs, wrong display, a talking protagonist). Following Merleau-Ponty's claim that art records subjective experience, the chapter treats Levine's team as artistic phenomenologists whose design question 'What is this experience we are trying to make?' turned Columbia and Elizabeth into phenomenological analyses to be read.

chapters.file: ch20 - Would You Kindly Evolve Today.md
chapters.relation: Ledder reads Plasmids and ADAM as human enhancement technology and stages the real bioethics debate: therapy versus enhancement, transhumanist enthusiasm (whole-brain emulation like Eleanor's ADAM-collecting, Sandberg's morphological freedom) against fears of Splicer-like superhumans and eugenics. The Rapture arms race, where your Electric Bolt Plasmid goes obsolete and forces further splicing, dramatizes the coercive spiral of competitive enhancement, while Habermas's objection that genetically designing children turns them into projections grounds the reading of Jack, Fontaine's purchased and conditioned embryo triggered by 'would you kindly', as a metaphor for engineered autonomy destroyed. The chapter closes with disability critiques: maybe the problem is not the body but the social barriers that 'disable' it, so changing society might beat changing flesh.

chapters.file: ch21 - This Is the End.md
chapters.relation: Muniz uses Dr. Steinman's surgical madness in the Medical Pavilion to test whether beauty and morality are entangled: Plato's Symposium makes beauty the value binding truth and goodness (Steinman's 'Goddess' of symmetry), Aristotle names order, symmetry, and definiteness the chief forms of beauty, and Keats's 'Beauty is truth' frames Steinman's descent into asymmetry-hating madness. Dewey's point that the young let the beautiful govern their behavior, plus the author's puppy-versus-rat classroom experiment, shows how the ugly get treated as morally worse, as in Steinman's 'moral obligation' to beautify. The Circus of Values vending machines frame the intrinsic-versus-extrinsic value distinction behind the Little Sister save-or-harvest dilemma, and the chapter concludes players must disentangle beauty from goodness and choose values for themselves.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Russian-American novelist-philosopher (1905-1982) whose Objectivism champions rational self-interest, laissez-faire capitalism, and art as a selective re-creation of reality; Andrew Ryan is her fictional male counterpart.
holes.why: Chapter 4's entire argument about Rapture as the fate of Galt's Atlantis, and the book's framing question of whether BioShock refutes Rand, turns on her biography, Atlas Shrugged, and her theory of art.

holes.name: Objectivism (rational self-interest)
holes.what: Rand's philosophy that enlightened rational self-interest and unregulated capitalism are moral ideals, with 'parasites' who live off others as the enemy.
holes.why: Chapter 4 argues the game indicts not Objectivism itself but Ryan's failure to integrate emotion into it, and Ryan's ideology, propaganda, and 'sweat of his brow' speech in later chapters are all Objectivism in action.

holes.name: Many-Worlds Interpretation (Everett)
holes.what: Hugh Everett III's reading of quantum mechanics on which the wave function never collapses and every measurement branches the universe into equally real parallel worlds.
holes.why: Chapter 9 treats BioShock Infinite's tears and constants-and-variables multiverse as Everett's many-worlds made real, which is what blocks alternate possibilities and generates the chapter's transworld moral responsibility thesis.

holes.name: Frankfurt Cases (against alternate possibilities)
holes.what: Harry Frankfurt's counterexamples showing an agent can be morally responsible even when a counterfactual intervener would have made it impossible to do otherwise, refuting the Principle of Alternate Possibilities.
holes.why: Chapter 9's central move is modeling Jack's 'would you kindly' conditioning and the player's confined choices as a Frankfurt case with Atlas as the prior-sign intervener, so responsibility survives without alternative possibilities.

holes.name: Carl Schmitt
holes.what: German political theorist (1888-1985) who grounded 'the political' in the friend-enemy distinction and defined the sovereign as 'he who decides on the exception'.
holes.why: Chapter 14 uses Schmitt's concepts of political founding, antagonism, and sovereignty as its entire framework for analyzing Columbia's secession, its racism, the Vox Populi's tyranny, and the ending's elimination of DeWitt.

holes.name: Human Enhancement (transhumanism vs bioconservatism)
holes.what: The bioethics debate over technologies that improve human bodies and minds beyond species-typical functioning, spanning therapy-versus-enhancement lines, transhumanist defenses, morphological freedom, and Habermas-style objections to designing children.
holes.why: Chapter 20 reads Plasmids and ADAM precisely as human enhancement technologies and stages the whole pro-and-con debate, including the enhancement arms race, designer children, and disability critiques of the 'normal functioning' ideal.

holes.name: Philosophy of Beauty (beauty and morality)
holes.what: Classical and pragmatist accounts of beauty, from Plato's Symposium and Aristotle's order-and-symmetry to the question of whether aesthetic value shapes moral judgment.
holes.why: Chapter 21 reads Dr. Steinman's surgical madness through Plato's and Aristotle's accounts of beauty and Dewey on aesthetic influence, arguing BioShock links beauty to goodness in ways players must learn to disentangle.
